\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Equal singleton Fourier coefficients]
\lean{FABL.HasEqualSingletonFourierCoefficients}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p060-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p135-b001
}
\label{FABL.HasEqualSingletonFourierCoefficients}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.fourierCoeff}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f$ be a Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional
Boolean cube with sign-valued output. The singleton Fourier coefficients of the
associated real-valued function are equal: for every pair of coordinates
$i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the coefficient indexed by $\{i\}$ equals the coefficient
indexed by $\{j\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Negating a function negates its coefficient sum]
\lean{FABL.sum_fourierCoeff_singleton_neg}
\label{FABL.sum_fourierCoeff_singleton_neg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal_neg, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.signValue, FABL.sum_fourierCoeff_singleton_eq_expect_mul_sum_signValue}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$. The sum of the singleton
Fourier coefficients of the pointwise negative of $f$ is the negative of the
corresponding sum for $f$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$ be a Boolean function, interpreted as real-valued by its
sign. The absolute value of the sum of its degree-one Fourier coefficients is at most
the sum of the degree-one Fourier coefficients of the majority function, which outputs
the sign of the sum of the input coordinates (with zero assigned the positive sign).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Level-One Weight Bound by Majority Influence]
\lean{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_le_totalInfluence_majority_sq_div}
\label{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_le_totalInfluence_majority_sq_div}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.HasEqualSingletonFourierCoefficients, FABL.abs_sum_fourierCoeff_singleton_le_majority, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel, FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_eq_sum_singleton, FABL.majority, FABL.majority_monotone, FABL.totalInfluence, FABL.totalInfluence_eq_sum_fourierCoeff_singleton_of_monotone, FABL.totalInfluence_nonneg}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be a Boolean function whose singleton Fourier coefficients
are all equal, and suppose $n>0$. Its level-one Fourier weight is at most the square of
the total influence of majority on the $n$-dimensional cube, divided by $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Level-one Fourier weight of odd majority]
\lean{FABL.totalInfluence_majority_odd_sq_div_card}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{

\difficulty{3}
For every integer $m\ge 0$, the square of the total influence of majority on the
$(2m+1)$-dimensional Boolean cube, divided by $2m+1$, equals its Fourier weight at level
one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Vanishing reciprocal sequence]
\lean{FABL.three_div_nat_isLittleO_one}
\label{FABL.three_div_nat_isLittleO_one}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
As $n\to\infty$ through the natural numbers, the sequence $3/n$ is little-$o$ of the
constant sequence $1$; equivalently, $3/n$ tends to zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Asymptotic Level-One Fourier Weight Bound]
\lean{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_eventually_le_two_div_pi_add}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p060-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p063-b003
}
\label{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_eventually_le_two_div_pi_add}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.HasEqualSingletonFourierCoefficients, FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel, FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_le_two_div_pi_add_three_div_card, FABL.three_div_nat_isLittleO_one}
\difficulty{4}
For each natural number $n$, let $f_n:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be a Boolean function, and
suppose all its singleton Fourier coefficients are equal. For every $\varepsilon>0$, for
all sufficiently large $n$, its level-one Fourier weight is at most $2/\pi+\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}
